feed.title: Economics — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Atlas of Economic Complexity
entry.summary: The Harvard Growth Lab’s atlas visualising a country’s export structure and economic complexity. Unlike raw trade data it comes with derived measures such as the complexity index, which reads growth potential off the export basket.

entry.title: Bureau of Economic Analysis
entry.summary: The official US publisher of GDP, national accounts, personal income and international trade data. Unlike BLS it focuses on production and income accounts rather than the labour market; it has GDP tables by state and industry.

entry.title: Bureau of Labor Statistics
entry.summary: The official US source for employment, unemployment, wages and consumer inflation (CPI). It publishes many series you see on FRED; unlike FRED it goes down to occupation, industry and region breakdowns. It has a public API.

entry.title: NBER Data
entry.summary: Datasets released by NBER researchers: macroeconomic history, CPS extracts, patent data. Unlike NBER Working Papers it is the data behind the papers, not the papers themselves, which makes it useful for reproducible economics.

entry.title: UN Comtrade
entry.summary: The UN database of countries’ merchandise trade by product (HS code) and partner. Unlike national customs statistics it collects countries into one structure, so trade between two countries can be checked against both sides’ reports; free use has limits.

entry.title: UNDP Human Development Data Center
entry.summary: The data centre for the UNDP’s Human Development Index and its related composite indices (inequality, gender, poverty). Unlike income-only GDP data it folds health and education into the same index.

entry.title: US Census Bureau
entry.summary: The official publisher of US population, household, housing and business statistics, home to the American Community Survey and the economic censuses. Unlike aggregators such as FRED it goes down to county and neighbourhood level; it offers raw tables and an API.

entry.title: BIS — Bank for International Settlements
entry.summary: The central bank of central banks, publishing global financial statistics and research papers. Unlike market-data sites it focuses on systemic and cross-border banking data.

entry.title: EconJobMarket
entry.summary: A platform managing academic economics job applications in one place, collecting applications and reference letters. A standard application flow instead of scattered emails.

entry.title: EconLib
entry.summary: A library holding an economics encyclopedia, essays and full texts of classic economics works. Unlike current data portals it offers concepts and theory rather than data, with a distinctly free-market editorial stance.

entry.title: Economics Stack Exchange
entry.summary: An economics Q&A site where you can ask experts about concepts and models. Unlike a forum, voting and editing surface the best answer.

entry.title: FRED
entry.summary: The St. Louis Fed’s economic database — 800,000+ US and world series, with charting and an API. Unlike raw statistical releases, the browse-plot-download flow lives in one place.

entry.title: IDEAS / RePEc
entry.summary: One of the largest databases of economics publications — over two million papers, working papers and software items. Unlike Google Scholar it is field-specific: it indexes economics alone and derives author and institution rankings.

entry.title: IGM Experts Panel
entry.summary: A panel where leading economists vote whether they agree with topical policy questions. Unlike a single expert’s view it shows at a glance where the consensus sits.

entry.title: IMF Data
entry.summary: The IMF’s macro data — the standard reference for balance of payments, exchange rates and debt. It leans more to monetary and fiscal statistics than the World Bank.

entry.title: JOE · Job Openings for Economists
entry.summary: The American Economic Association’s official job board — the central place for the academic economics market. Unlike general job sites it is economics positions only.

entry.title: Khan Academy · Ekonomi
entry.summary: A free video-and-exercise set teaching the basics of micro, macro and finance from scratch. Unlike university courses it targets the introductory level and intuition.

entry.title: Marginal Revolution
entry.summary: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok’s daily economics blog — among the most-read in the field. Against news it offers a short, frequent stream of commentary through an economist’s lens.

entry.title: MIT OCW · İktisat
entry.summary: Over 100 courses across every major field of economics in MIT’s open courseware. Unlike YouTube playlists these are full course structures with prerequisites and reading lists.

entry.title: NBER Working Papers
entry.summary: Working papers from the US National Bureau of Economic Research — most later appear in peer-reviewed journals. Unlike the journals it lets you read leading research months before publication; bear in mind they have not yet been peer-reviewed.

entry.title: OECD Data
entry.summary: Official OECD statistics across member economies, standardised for cross-country comparison straight from the source. Unlike general data aggregators the data is standardised and comes directly from the official source.

entry.title: OpenStax · Principles of Economics
entry.summary: A free, openly licensed textbook for introductory university economics. Unlike commercial texts it is free and regularly updated, with PDF, web and print editions.

entry.title: Our World in Data
entry.summary: A university-backed research publication presenting long-run data on the economy, population, health and environment as interactive charts. Unlike raw data portals it pairs the data with narrative and context, and every chart is freely reusable.

entry.title: QuantEcon
entry.summary: Open-source lectures and libraries for computational economics (Python and Julia). Unlike pure theory it teaches building and solving models in code — widely used in quantitative economics.

entry.title: RePEc
entry.summary: A network of services for economics researchers: bibliography, working-paper feeds, blog aggregator. Unlike a single archive it is distributed volunteer infrastructure; IDEAS is its front end, repec.org the system behind it.

entry.title: RFE · Resources for Economists
entry.summary: A guide of thousands of links for economists, maintained by the American Economic Association. A directory curated by the field itself rather than random search.

entry.title: SSRN Economics
entry.summary: A preprint archive of economics working papers. Unlike NBER it is not tied to one institution: anyone can upload, so it is broader but less filtered.

entry.title: Statista
entry.summary: A statistics portal aggregating market and survey data across industries with sourcing. Unlike primary data sources it collects scattered figures into one chart; access to the raw data and downloads is mostly paid.

entry.title: Trading Economics
entry.summary: Gathers macro indicators — GDP, inflation, rates — for 196 countries in one dashboard with historical series and forecasts. Unlike official portals that cover one country, it offers cross-country comparison and forecasts.

entry.title: VoxEU / CEPR
entry.summary: A stream of columns where researchers explain their own work to a policy audience (CEPR). Unlike a working paper it drops the jargon and makes the finding accessible.

entry.title: World Bank Data
entry.summary: International macroeconomic time series, country by country. Unlike individual statistics offices it is comparable: hundreds of indicators under common definitions in one place.

entry.title: Visual Capitalist
entry.summary: A publication turning economic and technology data into infographics. Not a raw data source — its contribution is making magnitudes comparable.
